senses.gloss:
Vāc
(‘speech’)
------------------------------------------
Vāc or Vāk—also known as Ambhṛṇī—is one of the Vedic women-sages to whom the Devīsūkta (Ṛgveda 10.125) was revealed. See DEVĪSŪKTA for details.
Vāc (vāk) as speech has been described in the Vedic literature in various ways.
The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (4.1.3.16) divides speech into four kinds: that of human beings, of animals, of birds and of small creeping things. The Taittirīya Saṁhitā (6.4.7.3) says that इन्द्र made the articulate speech. It also refers to three musical instruments—tūṇava (flute), vīṇā (lute) and दुन्दुभि (kettle-drum) (ibid 6.1.4.1).
Coming to the human speech, that of the कुरु-Pāñcālas was considered very good and fit to be learnt by others (vide Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 3.2.3.15; Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa 7.6). The असुरस् were known for their barbarian speech (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 3.2.1.23,24) and hence had to be avoided.
Sometimes speech is categorised as daivī (divine) and mānuṣī (human). For instance Om is daivī whereas tathā is mānuṣī (vide Kāṭhaka Saṁhitā 14.5). A ब्राह्मण is said to know both. Probably this categorisation refers to the language used in Vedic rituals and in daily life.
As regards the evolution of speech from the subtle to the gross stages see PARĀ for details.
Vāc is one of the names of the goddess सरस्वती. (See SARASVATĪ also.)

Vācaspati
(‘master of speech’)
------------------------------------------
This is one of the several names of बृहस्पति, the गुरु of the gods.
See BṚHASPATI.

vacanas
(‘[poetical] sayings’)
------------------------------------------
The वचनस् are a special kind of literary compositions in the Kannada language. They are religious or semi-religious lyrics in the local colloquial language. They appear like prose but are flavoured with poetical grace. The credit of discovering and introducing these goes to the Vīraśaiva saints like बसवेश्वर (12th century A. D.), Allamaprabhu (12th century A. D.), Akkamahādevī (A. D. 1130-1166) and a host of others.
The primary purpose of these वचनस् is to carry the essential teachings of philosophy, religion, मोरलित्य् and social values to the common folk in their own language.
Though the number of the vacana-kāras (composers of the वचनस्) is quite large and their compositions run into thousands, the names of a few—the more important ones—may be mentioned here:
Akkamahādevī(12th century A. D.; 365 वचनस्) Allamaprabhu(12th century A. D.; 1294 वचनस्) Ambigara Cauḍayya(12th century A. D.; 200 वचनस्) Āydakki Mārayya (50 वचनस्) Basaveśvara(12th century A. D.; 1200 वचनस्) Cennabasavaṇṇa(12th century A. D.; 1500 वचनस्) Devara Dāsimayya(circa A. D. 1135; 142 वचनस्) Haḍapada Appaṇṇa(12th century A. D.; 222 वचनस्) Hāvina Hāḷa Kallayya(12th century A. D.; 60 वचनस्) Maḍivāḷa Mācayya(12th century A. D.; 345 वचनस्) Uriliṅga Peddi(A. D. 1180; 294 वचनस्).

vācika
(‘pertaining to speech’)
------------------------------------------
This word has been used more as an adjective than as a noun.
As a noun it means any news or a message sent by word or mouth.
As an adjective its meaning changes according to the word it qualifies. For instance:
Vācika-तपस् is तपस् or austerity of speech. According to the Bhagavadgītā (17.15) it is a speech which is true, sweet and brings about nothing but good. It should be without agitation and anxiety. Study of one’s own branch of Veda and repetition of the divine name also comes under this definition.
Vācika-doṣas or defects of speech are: telling lies, castigating others, deeply hurting the feelings of others, praising oneself and carrying tales about others.
Vācika-pāpas or sins committed by word of mouth are: speaking very harshly, telling lies especially to hurt others, finding fault, and raving.
